newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe irked by fresh coalition sniping.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe irked by fresh coalition sniping.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's drive to recapture the political initiative, unite his fractious coalition and break a national mood of gloom with a tax-cutting plan has run into early trouble.

Renewed sniping erupted in the conservative coalition at the weekend, an opinion poll on Monday showed most voters are deeply sceptical of his tax plan and Juppe's own talk of electoral reform has confused the political debate.
A CSA institute poll in the business daily La Tribune showed a small plurality -- 42-39 percent -- in favour of the income tax cuts that Juppe announced on television last Thursday.

But it also found that 69 percent thought the proposed reform would not restore confidence, 71 percent felt it would not revive flagging growth and 80 percent believed it would not help bring down near-record 12.5 percent unemployment.
Many voters appeared convinced by opposition arguments that the tax cuts would favour the rich, while the general public would pay in higher duty on tobacco, alcohol and petrol.
Public doubts about Juppe's strategy were reflected in a fresh crossfire of criticism within his centre-right coalition.
Former interior minister Charles Pasqua said the country was "on the wrong course" and ex-finance minister Alain Madelin called the tax reform insufficient to revive a stagnant economy.

Francois Leotard, leader of the UDF party, junior partner to Juppe's Gaullist RPR in government, responded to the prime minister's call for greater coalition discipline by saying the alliance was not a "barracks".
The prime minister showed his irritation with such criticism on Monday, telling a Radio Luxembourg interviewer: "The French people are fed up with this petty Sunday sniping."
While saying the coalition was "united and coherent", Juppe reacted to Leotard's "barracks" jibe by saying he did not see himself as an army sergeant-major.
"Between a barracks and a holiday camp, there are perhaps more important things to do in politics," he added.
Juppe gave Pasqua short shrift on Monday, ending a meeting with him after just 15 minutes.
Pasqua, popular among right-wing, Eurosceptical Gaullists, told reporters:"It was a conversation marked, in the language of diplomacy, by a friendly atmosphere and great mutual frankness."
"The climate was good, the receptiveness less so," he added.
Political analysts said Juppe had blurred his own message by launching a debate about electoral reform just as he was trying to focus public attention on tax cuts.
Aides said he did so unintentionally in a remark at a coalition lunch last Thursday which was leaked to the media.

The prime minister confirmed publicly on Monday he wanted the political parties to consider introducing an element of proportional representation alongside the current constituency voting system for the next parliamentary election in March 1998.

Just as the late president Francois Mitterrand switched to proportional representation in 1986 to limit the damage of his Socialist party's anticipated defeat, conservative President Jacques Chirac now seemed keen to change the rules to minimise his own coalition's potential losses in 1998, analysts said.

But Juppe appeared to rule out a proposal by Pasqua to elect deputies by proportional representation in heavily-populated areas while keeping single-member constituencies elsewhere -- a plan that would hurt the opposition Socialists in their urban strongholds and protect the centre-right in its rural bastions.
Juppe said he opposed "creating two categories of voters in France". Officials said the idea was anyway almost certainly unconstitutional.
